about.intro: I grew up in Dehradun, studied business at Hartwell College of Commerce in Dunmore Heights and joined Pinewick Paper & Print as an inside sales rep in July 2019, at a desk beside Tilly Brandt, who runs the office while the regional manager believes he does. I booked account visits for nearly three years, cut the company quote from six pages to one, and became an Account Executive for schools, offices and print shops in 2022. I took the Top Seller plaque in FY23 and FY25; Marla Finch took FY24 and has mentioned it since. In 2025 I started a diploma at Ashgrove Institute of Commerce to study the money and strategy behind large contracts, then spent spring 2026 on contract at Brightline Packaging.
about.now: Editing the next Closing Time episode, writing fresh jokes for the Tuesday open mic, and rehearsing bhangra steps for the harvest fair.

cold-call-playbook.context: Pinewick Paper & Print quoted reorders with a six-page template the regional manager had designed around a motivational poster. It covered terms, shipping zones and a mission statement before it reached a price.
cold-call-playbook.problem: Buyers told me they skimmed to page four and then rang to ask what it cost. A quote took 25 minutes to build and about 22 in 100 became orders.
what_i_did: Read 120 of my own sent quotes and marked where each buyer rang back with a question.
Drafted a one-page version: price at the top, delivery date, one named local customer as reference and one clear next step.
Asked Tilly Brandt, who proofreads everything that leaves the building, to test it on five customers who rang reception.
Ran a six-week split test: half of my pod's quotes used each format, tracked by order-desk number.
Presented the result to Gordie Pruitt, who renamed it Project ONE-PAGER-DRIVE and rolled it out to three teams.

decisions.choice: Name a local customer on the quote
decisions.why: Buyers trusted a school or print shop they knew more than any guarantee we could print.

decisions.choice: A split test, not a Monday rollout
decisions.why: The regional manager wanted to switch everyone at once. Six weeks with the same reps on both formats meant nobody could blame luck or Marla Finch's territory.

cold-call-playbook.learned: Buyers did not want less information. They wanted the price first and the rest on request. The terms page is still there, as a link.
cold-call-playbook.next: Add a one-click reorder link for customers who buy the same stock every term.

district-chain-deal.context: Millbrook School District runs 14 schools across Larchmont County and bought paper, forms and printed materials from five suppliers, each with its own account and delivery schedule. The district's staff are anonymised here.
district-chain-deal.problem: The district office could not see what each school spent, and teachers ran out of paper in the second week of term. Their estimate was that about three orders in ten arrived late or incomplete, and nobody owned the fix.
what_i_did: Ran discovery at three schools: spent two days with school secretaries and the district office and mapped every order from request to delivery.

Mapped 9 stakeholders, from a school secretary to the finance director, and sat down with every one of them. Tilly Brandt on our reception knew which front offices actually answered the phone, and told me.
Proposed a paid 8-week delivery pilot at three schools instead of a district-wide switch, and three measures of success signed off beforehand.
Wrote the business case for the finance director from the pilot data: on-time delivery, emergency re-orders and spend per pupil. Dennis Hale checked every figure and rounded it his way.
Agreed a phased rollout and a two-year price hold, with the district giving us a case study and one reference call.

decisions.choice: A paid pilot, not free samples
decisions.why: Free samples had stalled with another district the year before. A small fee got the operations manager to give the pilot a named owner.

decisions.choice: Lead with late deliveries, not price lists
decisions.why: The finance director cared about one number: how many orders arrived late and forced an emergency purchase. That was the pilot's main measure.

decisions.choice: Trade a price hold for a case study
decisions.why: Procurement asked for 12% off. A 2-year price hold cost us less and gave Gordie Pruitt his first district reference, which he promptly turned into a whiteboard acronym.

district-chain-deal.learned: Things sped up once the district's operations manager began showing the pilot figures to her own finance director. From then on I backed up her case and the meetings shrank.
district-chain-deal.next: Expand to the district's sports clubs and the nearby adult-education centre, where the same ordering problem exists at a smaller order size.

peoplely-manufacturing.context: Brightline Packaging makes corrugated cartons and shipping boxes for regional producers. Its key-account team covered grocery chains but nobody worked food and drink producers with 200 or more employees across three counties.
peoplely-manufacturing.problem: The team did not know which producers were worth a call. Plans were one-line notes, and the last campaign sent one email to 600 inboxes and got four replies.
what_i_did: Built a list of 40 producers from county registers and plant-visit notes, scored on carton spend, shipping routes and number of buyers.
Wrote a one-page plan for each: who buys, who signs, what they ship and what could go wrong.
Ran outbound by phone and LinkedIn to procurement leads and plant managers, with each message written for that plant.
Reviewed every first-meeting note weekly with the key-account managers and dropped accounts that were a poor fit.
Handed 5 qualified opportunities to the account team with the plan, contacts and agreed next step.

decisions.choice: Forty deep plans, not 600 shallow emails
decisions.why: The earlier campaign proved volume did not work here. A short, specific message to a named buyer got a reply far more often.

decisions.choice: Qualify on who signs, not who replies
decisions.why: A friendly plant manager with no budget felt like progress but was not. I counted an opportunity only once the person who signs had agreed to a meeting.

peoplely-manufacturing.learned: Plans with a named signer and a named blocker turned into meetings. Generic plans did not, even with a good opening line.
peoplely-manufacturing.next: Take the same plan template to the bakery and beverage segments and test it against two reps working without it.

forecast-review.context: Each Monday the regional manager asked for a commit number and wrote the total on the whiteboard under a four-letter acronym that changed monthly. Reps gave numbers based on mood.
forecast-review.problem: Monthly commit error ran about ±31%. That made stock ordering a guessing game for Wendell Odom's warehouse and gave Dennis Hale a rounding grievance at every month-end.
what_i_did: Exported four quarters of closed deals and compared the stage each deal was in with how it ended.
Found that deals sat at "proposal" for weeks with no reply from the buyer, and still counted in the commit.
Wrote 6 exit criteria for each stage, including a buyer-confirmed date and a named signer.
Built the sheet in Google Sheets with Dennis, who insisted that every figure round half up to the cent, and was right.
Ran it as a 20-minute Monday review for the 8-rep team for three quarters.

decisions.choice: Exit criteria the buyer confirms, not the rep
decisions.why: A stage only moved when something the buyer said or did could be pointed to. Optimism stopped counting as evidence.
Dennis's rule: keep full figures all the way through and round only in the final column. It ended the month-end argument about two-cent differences.

results.note: the whole AE team by the third quarter

forecast-review.learned: Reps filled the sheet in honestly once it stopped being used against them. The acronym stayed on the whiteboard, but the numbers came from the sheet.
forecast-review.next: Add stock lead times from the warehouse so the forecast also tells Wendell what to order.
forecast-review.my_role: Account Executive, wrote the sheet and chaired the review

sales-sprint.context: Ashgrove Institute of Commerce runs a two-day Sales Showdown each year. Teams get a case about a regional paper wholesaler that wants to consolidate suppliers, and they sell a multi-year contract to a mock buyer.
sales-sprint.problem: Past winners had polished slides and thin discovery. The judges scored whether the team found the buyer's real priority, and few teams asked enough questions to find it.
what_i_did: Ran a 40-minute discovery session with the mock buyer, played by a lecturer, and found that delivery reliability mattered more than price.
Split the team's roles: one on questions, one on numbers, one taking notes and one negotiating.
Built a 20-minute pitch around three numbers the buyer had confirmed in discovery.
Rehearsed the negotiation against a classmate playing the toughest buyer he could think of, with a stopwatch.

decisions.choice: Spend half the prep time on discovery
decisions.why: The case rewarded finding the priority over polishing slides, and every other team did the opposite.

decisions.choice: Concede on payment terms, hold on price
decisions.why: Payment terms cost the wholesaler little and mattered to the buyer. Price was where the margin was.

sales-sprint.learned: The pitch won on the questions we asked in the first round, not on the slides we showed in the second.
sales-sprint.next: Run the same discovery-first rehearsal with next year's teams, with a buyer who changes their mind halfway.

agri-territory.context: Hollis Wholesale supplies stationery and school supplies to small shops across Dunmore County. Four field reps visit the shops by van, and our class team was given six weeks to improve their routes.
agri-territory.problem: Reps chose their next stop by memory, so vans crossed the county twice in a day. Visits per rep per day averaged 7 and the drive between shops took longer than the visits did.
what_i_did: Mapped 410 shops from the wholesaler's order history, with delivery windows and typical order size.
Grouped the shops into daily routes by area, so each rep stayed in one part of the county per day.
Tested the new routes with two reps for four weeks and logged each visit in a shared sheet.
Interviewed the reps on what the map got wrong, and moved two shops that closed for lunch.
Presented the results and a one-page route guide to the owner.

decisions.choice: Fix routes by area, not by customer value
decisions.why: Ranking by value sent reps back and forth across the county. Area routes saved drive time, and big shops still got visited every week.

decisions.choice: Pilot with two reps, not four
decisions.why: A smaller test let us compare against the other two reps on the old routes at the same time.

agri-territory.learned: The reps knew which shops closed at lunch and which owners liked a visit on Fridays. The route map was better for including it.
agri-territory.next: Add delivery-van timing so that sales visits and drop-offs share the same route.

chart.title: Visits per rep per day, pilot routes

closing-time.context: Closing Time is a fortnightly podcast I host. Each episode has one guest, usually a shop owner or buyer, telling the story of an order that went wrong and what the supplier could have done.
closing-time.problem: Suppliers rarely hear why buyers stopped ordering. Shop owners have the stories but no stage, and sales teams have the stage but no stories.
what_i_did: Invited guests from my own accounts and from the Larchmont Falls trade fair, and sent a one-page brief before each recording.
Recorded on weekends, about 30 minutes each, in the Pinewick stockroom after asking Wendell Odom, who gave a philosophical yes.
Edited in Audacity on Sunday nights and published to Spotify and Apple Podcasts every second Monday.
Wrote a one-page takeaway for each episode so listeners in sales could use the lesson at work.

decisions.choice: Orders that went wrong, not success stories
decisions.why: Guest bookeds were more candid about a late delivery than about a win, and the lessons were more specific.
Short episodes fit a lunch break and kept guests from drifting into the weather.

closing-time.learned: Guest bookeds tell a better story when they are asked what they did next, not what went wrong. I now use the same question in discovery calls.
closing-time.next: Invite two suppliers and a buyer to the same episode, and let them argue about whose fault it was.

flow.title: One episode, every two weeks
steps: A shop owner or buyer, found through my accounts
One page, emailed ahead of recording

objection-drills.context: New inside reps at Pinewick spent their first weeks reading product sheets. Nobody practised the hard moments out loud, such as a buyer saying the price is too high.
objection-drills.problem: It took a new rep about six weeks to book a first account visit, and some did not make a call with a price in it before week three.
what_i_did: Wrote 6 objection cards from the real calls I had heard, with price and delivery at the top of the pile.
Ran a 30-minute drill every Friday: one card, one stopwatch, and two reps swapping roles as buyer and seller.
Asked Priya Raman in HR to put the drill into the new-starter schedule, which she did without comment, as she does with everything.
Tracked the weeks to a first booked visit for each cohort in a Notion page.
Handed the cards to a colleague when I moved to the Account Executive team.

decisions.choice: Drill on Fridays, not in onboarding week
decisions.why: By Friday new reps had heard real objections and had something to practise against.
Playing the buyer showed reps how short and blunt the real objection is.

objection-drills.learned: Reps got better when they heard their own answer back. The cards mattered less than the stopwatch.
objection-drills.next: Record two sample answers per card so reps can hear a good one before they try.
